---
title: "Factors"
---

In statistical data analysis, we often need to represent categorical variables: data that fall into of discrete groups
or levels. Typical examples include nominal variables like {"male", "female"}, {"yes", "no"}, or political party
affiliation. In R, we use *factors* to represent categorical variables in our data.

An R factor is a special kind of object that encodes a categorical variable's grouping information in a consistent way
that R functions know how to handle. When we use a categorical variable as part of a statistical model or visualization,
R needs to apply special processing to make the variable correctly represent groups or levels. Factors trigger this
special processing, so they are particularly important for modeling and plotting functions.

## Where Factors Fit

If you've completed the earlier modules in this series, you already have all the background information you need to
understand factors. Recall the hierarchy of data structures you've built up so far:

1. Vectors (dimensionless, same data type)
1. Matrices (two-dimensional, same data type)
1. Lists (dimensionless, mixed data types)
1. Data Frames (*seemingly* two-dimensional, mixed data types)

Factors add to this hierarchy, but not by allowing more dimensions or more heterogeneous data. Rather, factors add
*meaning* by incorporating additional metadata in the form of *levels* attribute that tells R how to
interpret the grouping structure represented by the factor.

::: knowledge-check

Why might it be a problem if R treated a "yes"/"no" survey response the same way it treats an ordinary numeric
measurement?

:::
